title: Anger, the burning thief
hookLine: krodh burns the one who holds it; righteous anger is guided by compassion

lines: A COAL IN A BARE HAND.
cards: A coal, picked up bare-handed to throw at someone. Before it ever reaches them, whose hand is already burning?
The Guru Granth Sahib names anger, krodh, among the five thieves living inside the body, the thieves you met early on this path. This one doesn't break in.
It flares up from inside, and the first thing it burns is the one holding it. Yet the Gurus also spoke fiercely against cruelty. So which is it?
Today: anger, and the second before it.

teach.b: First, Guru Arjan speaks to anger directly. In one of his saloks in the Granth he addresses it like a person. In paraphrase: O anger, root of strife, compassion never rises in you.
Then, the saloks go on, it takes people over and makes them dance to its tune. It doesn't just add heat. It pushes compassion out of the room.
Remember the Japji's bull a few days ago: dharma is the son of compassion. Anger shoves the mother out of her chair. Second, Farid's answer.
In paraphrase: Farid, answer evil with good; don't fill your mind with anger. Then your body won't fall sick, and you'll gain everything. Notice the body.
Farid knows anger wears down the one who holds it first. Third, the other anger. The Gurus were not quiet in the face of wrong.
Guru Nanak cried out against the cruelty of an invading army; we heard that protest days ago. The difference is what steers it. Krodh is anger for me: my pride hurt, my plan blocked.

teach.h: FIERCE FOR OTHERS, GUIDED BY COMPASSION.
teach.b: The fierceness the Gurus show is for others, and it's guided by compassion, not by the thief. Fourth, the gap. Anger is fast.
The tradition slows it with remembering, Simran, and in plain terms, a breath.
One breath before the send button. In that gap, compassion gets a chance to come back to its chair. Back to the coal: one breath can be long enough to notice it's in your own hand, and set it down.

how: Sikhs name krodh, anger, among the five thieves, kaam, krodh, lobh, moh and ahankar, and meet them through Naam Simran, the remembrance of the Lord, and the company of the sangat.

o: a fault that only shows in loud shouting
a righteous fire that should always be let out
krodh: a thief that burns the one who holds it

games.q: what's inside the teaching on anger: tap the pairs.

s: the Gurus never spoke fiercely against wrong
Guru Nanak cried out against an invading army's cruelty; that fierceness was for others and guided by compassion.
Farid links anger with the body falling sick
don't fill your mind with anger, and the body won't fall sick.
Guru Arjan says compassion rises in anger
his salok says compassion never rises in it.

games.q: someone wrongs you, and you're Farid. what does his couplet say to do?
o: answer evil with good, and don't fill your mind with anger.
games.why: Farid says answer evil with good; then the body won't fall sick, and you'll gain everything.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing that reliably irritates you, a slow driver, a certain tone, a dish left in the sink, and let a little of the heat come. Notice where it lands in your body: jaw, chest, hands.
Then take one slow breath, all the way in and out, before you think a single word about it, and watch what the heat does when it's given breaths instead of words.

wordCard.voice: Anger. Krodh, one of the five thieves: it burns the one who holds it and pushes compassion out; the fierceness the Gurus honor is guided by compassion. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: krodh, anger, one of the five thieves the Granth names.

carryVoice: Your line: breathe first. One breath is room enough for compassion to come back. See you tomorrow.
